fixes.explanation: Twelve it is, baker. Luke says that when He was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the Feast. So this trip is the same yearly trip, just with a twelve-year-old along. Same Feast as always, and this one is about to be anything but routine.

Eight is a fair guess, but the text gives a different number. Luke says Jesus was twelve years old on this trip. Luke says His parents went every year, but he doesn't say whether Jesus came along on the earlier trips. This is the trip Luke tells us about.

Thirty is close to the age Luke gives later, when Jesus begins His ministry. He says Jesus was about thirty (Luke 3:23). That's a long way down the road from this scene. Here, Luke says He was twelve years old. So picture a boy, not a grown man, standing in the middle of all this.
Close, but the text says the opposite. Luke writes that His parents were unaware He had stayed. They assumed He was in their company and traveled on. That's why the search starts later.

Yes, that's where they start. Luke says they traveled on for a day before they began to look for Him among their relatives and friends. They had been assuming He was in their company. So they started with the people they knew.
That's it, baker. Luke says that when they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him. They didn't give up on Him. That tells you plenty.

Waiting sounds calm, but Luke doesn't say they did that. When they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him. They went looking for Him. Later His mother says they had been anxiously searching (Luke 2:48).
Seven is a bigger number than the one Luke gives. The text says that finally, after three days, they found Him. So hold on to that number three.
Forty is a big number, and a lot of Bible stories use it, but this isn't one of them. Luke says that after three days they found Him. Three is the number in this verse.

Yes, the temple courts. Luke says they found Him there, sitting among the teachers. I once tore my whole bakery apart looking for my chef's hat, and it was on my head the entire time. Their search ended with a far bigger surprise than mine.

The Pool of Bethesda is a real place in Jerusalem (John 5:2), but it's not where this story ends up. Luke says they found Him in the temple courts. That's where Jesus was sitting among the teachers. So the answer is the temple, not the pool.

The Mount of Olives is a good guess, but Luke doesn't send anyone there in this story. He says they found Him in the temple courts. Jesus was sitting among the teachers. That's the spot where the search finally ends.

Right, baker. Luke says He was sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. Nothing in this verse says He was lecturing. And yet the next verse says all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers (Luke 2:47).

Luke doesn't mention a scroll in this scene. He says Jesus was listening to the teachers and asking them questions. The next verse adds that all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers (Luke 2:47). It's a quieter picture than reading aloud.

A psalm sounds like it could fit, but Luke doesn't say it. The text says He was sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions. That's the picture Luke gives for this verse. Nobody is said to be leading a psalm.
Astounded is the word. Luke says that all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. Notice it says all, not some.
Puzzled is a fair guess, but it isn't Luke's word. He says all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. Astounded is the word the text uses.
Annoyed isn't what Luke says. He says that all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers. Astounded is the reaction the text gives.

That's it, baker. Jesus asks, “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?” His mother had just told Him they'd been anxiously searching, and He answers with a question of His own. Luke says they did not understand the statement He was making to them (Luke 2:50).

Right, baker. Luke says, “But they did not understand the statement He was making to them.” Jesus was saying it right to them, and it still didn't click. I've nodded along to plenty of directions I didn't follow, so I get it.

True, baker. Luke says that Jesus went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. This is the same boy who just astounded the teachers (Luke 2:47). He goes home and is obedient to His parents.

Luke says the opposite. He writes that Jesus went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. The boy who astounded the teachers (Luke 2:47) went home with His parents and was obedient to them. Obedient is the word the text uses.
Treasures, baker. Luke says, “…treasured up all these things in her heart.” Treasured is the word Luke uses for what she did with them. I think it's the way you'd hold onto your favorite recipe card.
Jews and Greeks sounds like a fitting pair, but it isn't in this verse. Luke says Jesus grew in favor with God and man. That's the pair the text gives. So the answer is God and man.
